screens:
Lindmill has 300 people, one bridge and one bakery. The bakery is yours.

On Sunday, your little sister Lina gets married. The whole village is coming. You are making the bread.

Monday, four in the morning. The oven is hot. The village is still asleep.

You open your father's red book. He wrote every recipe in it by hand. He died three years ago. You turn to the page that says Wedding Bread.

A paper falls out. It was folded very small and pressed flat between the pages.

It is not a recipe.

It says: "I, Elias, owe Anton the miller this money. I will pay it back. If I cannot, my bakery is his."

Two names are signed under it: your father's and Anton's. And a third: Old Teo, who watched them sign. The date is 22 years ago.

The number on the paper is more than the bakery earns in three years.

On the back, in newer ink, in your father's hand: "I never paid. Pay this before any of you marries. Then tell your mother everything."

He put it here, on this page. He knew you would open it before a wedding.

Lina's wedding is in six days.

What you know about Anton:

He owns the mill by the river. You buy all your flour from him. In 22 years, he has never said one word about money.

His son, Milo, is the man Lina marries on Sunday.

At seven, Lina comes in with two cups of coffee. She is singing.

She holds up two ribbons for her hair. "Blue or white?"

At noon, Anton's cart brings the flour, like every Monday. He carries the sacks in himself.

He nods at you, the way he always does. Nothing in his face.

Night. Lina sits on the end of your bed, like when she was small.

"Six days," she says. "Are you happy for me?"

The paper is in your pocket. "Before any of you marries."

screens:
You told her last night. She did not cry. She read the paper twice, folded it, and gave it back.

"Does Milo know?" she asked. Then she went to her room and shut the door.

Tuesday, six in the morning. Her bed is empty. Her coat is gone.

From the bakery door, you can see the road to the mill. Someone small is walking fast. Lina.

The mill is loud. White dust hangs in the air. Milo comes out, smiling, with flour on his hands.

Lina gives him the paper. He reads it. The smile goes away.

"I didn't know," he says. He looks at Lina, then at you. "I swear I didn't know."

He walks into the office where his father sits. He shuts the door. Through the glass, you see Anton stand up.

Ten minutes. Then Anton comes out alone. He gives the paper back to you, not to Lina.

"Come to my house tonight," he says. "Just you."

All day, the bread does not rise right. Lina works next to you and says nothing.

Once, she puts her hand on your arm. Then she takes it away.

Night. Anton's kitchen is big and cold. He does not offer you tea.

"Yes, it is real," he says. "I have the other copy. Your father never paid. I never asked. My reasons are my own."

"Now I am asking. The big flour company in town sells cheaper than me. The mill is losing money. I need it."

He looks out of the window, at the river. "But I will not ruin my son's wedding. So I have an offer."

"Give half of the bakery to Milo and Lina. Call it a wedding gift. Then I burn both papers, and nobody ever speaks of it."

"Or pay me all of it, before the wedding. If not, the paper says the bakery is mine."

At noon, you take bread to Old Teo. He is past ninety. He sits on the bench by the well every day, and he sees everything.

His name is on the paper too.

You show him. He holds it close to his eyes for a long time.

"So Elias kept it," he says. "I watched them sign. Anton gave the money that same day. He did not even ask what it was for."

In the afternoon, Lina tries on her dress in the kitchen. Your mother cries a little and pins the dress. Lina turns and turns.

"Say something," she says to you. "You look like someone died."

Lina comes out from the back, still in her apron.

You show her. She reads it twice.

"When did you find this?"

You said yes. Anton shook your hand once, hard. "Good," he said. "It stays in the family."

Wednesday morning, you tell Lina and Milo. You think they will be glad. Lina puts her cup down very slowly.

"Half of your bakery?" she says. "As a gift to me?"

"No. A gift is something you want to give. This is a payment with my name on it."

Milo stands up. You have never seen him angry. He is angry now.

"I am not marrying a bakery," he says. He takes his coat and walks out, toward the mill.

By noon, the story is all over the mill. Milo shouted at his father in the yard, in front of the workers. In 26 years, he never once shouted at Anton.

Anton listened. Then he said one word: "Fine."

That evening, Anton comes to the bakery. He does not look at you.

"My son says no. So, no gift. Sunday, then. All the money. Or the bakery." He leaves the door open behind him.

"Then tell your mother everything." You cannot wait any more.

You sit with your mother at the kitchen table. You give her the paper.

She reads the front, then the back. She sits very still.

Then she brings down an old tea tin from the top shelf. "Twelve years of coins," she says. "For Lina's wedding feast. It is about half."
She puts her hand flat on the paper. "I know where this money went," she says. "I just never knew it came from Anton."

"Twenty-two years ago, the bank was going to take your uncle Beno's house. Beno, his wife, three small children. Then one morning it was all fine. Your father said a friend had helped."

"It was this. It was for Beno."

Through the window, you hear music from the café. Beno's accordion. Somebody is laughing. It is Beno.

On Sunday, he gives the family toast, in your father's place.

Thursday. You walk up the hill to Beno's house. His grandson is feeding the chickens.

Beno opens the door, laughing about something. Then he sees the paper in your hand, and he stops laughing.

He reads it at the kitchen table. His wife reads it over his shoulder.

"I'll sell the field," he says. "The one by the river. It is all I have. It is yours."

His wife stands in the door with her arms crossed. "That field is for our children," she says. Beno does not look at her.

Beno calls a man in town who buys land. They talk for a long time.

When he puts the phone down, his face is grey. "He will buy it. But the papers take a month. Nothing before Sunday."
So the field will come too late. You walk back down the hill alone. The tin is still half. The rest is still missing.

Back at the bakery, you work until dark. Your mother counts the tin again and again, as if the coins could grow.

Lina writes the names of the guests on little cards. Three hundred cards.
At ten, there is a soft knock at the back door. It is Milo. He looks over his shoulder before he comes in.

He puts an envelope on the table. It is thick.

"My savings," he says. "Since I was a boy. It is about half. With your mother's tin, it is all of it."

"Pay my father with this. Tell him you found the money. He will never know it is mine."

"And Lina?" you ask.

"She doesn't need to know. Nobody does. On Sunday we are one family anyway."

Someone knocks at the back door. Softly.

It is Beno. No accordion. No laugh. He has not been drinking. You can tell.

"Can I sit?" he says. He sits before you answer.

"I lied to you on Thursday," he says. "I always knew. Elias told me the day he paid. He made me promise never to pay him back. Just be a good father, he said."

"So I was. And I let him carry it. Twenty-two years."

"And it was me. At the café, on Thursday night. I drank, and I told them all. I wanted them to know Elias was a good man."

"I made it worse. I know."

He looks at his hands. "Tomorrow I am meant to give the toast, in his place."

"Do you still want me to?"

He does not see you. Or he acts like he does not.

Night. You sit in the bakery. The dough rests under white cloths. The square outside is empty. No tables. No lights.

Someone knocks at the back door. Softly.

It is Beno. No accordion. No laugh. He has not been drinking. You can tell.

"I lied to you on Thursday," he says. "I always knew. Elias told me the day he paid. He made me promise never to pay him back. Just be a good father, he said. So I was. And I let him carry it."

"And it was me. At the café, on Thursday night. I drank, and I told them all. I wanted them to know Elias was a good man."

"It was my debt. Now Lina has no feast. I know."

He looks at his hands. "Tomorrow I am meant to give the toast, in his place. Even at a small wedding."

"Do you still want me to?"

options.line: "Don't be," she says. But her voice is small.

options.text: Tell her it will still be beautiful.
options.line: "It will," she says. "You are making the bread."
He nods once. He does not turn round.
The water is loud under the bridge.

vote.question: Beno lied, and he talked. Tomorrow is the toast. What do you say?

A.label: Forgive him. Let him give the toast.
A.reason: He is your father's brother. Your father forgave him every day for 22 years.

B.label: Not yet. You give the toast.
B.reason: He lied to your face two days ago. Forgiving takes more than one night.

B.science: Forgiving can help the one who forgives. In one study, people thought of someone who hurt them. When they pictured forgiving, their heart rate and blood pressure stayed lower than when they went over the hurt.

screens:
Sunday. Four in the morning. The oven is hot. The red book is open at Wedding Bread.

Beno stayed all night. Now he is asleep on the flour sacks, snoring. You let him sleep.

By noon, the square is full. Three hundred people at the long tables. Lights in the walnut tree. Your bread is on every table, still warm.

Lina walks out in white. The whole village stands up.

Anton sits at the head table with his wife. He has not looked at you once.

The first dance is in an hour.

Beno stands up for the toast. He has his accordion, but he puts it down.

"My brother Elias paid my debt," he says to everyone. "Twenty-two years ago. I let him carry it. I never paid back one coin. Today I start."

He walks to Anton and puts a paper in front of him. The papers for his field by the river.

"It is not all of it," Beno says. "It is what I have."

The square is very quiet. Anton looks at the paper for a long time. Then he stands up.

"I never asked Elias for this money," he says. "Not once in twenty years. You all want to know why. Here is why."

"The summer after we signed, my boy fell into the river by the mill wheel. He was four. I could not reach him. Elias was bringing the bread. He jumped in."

Anton looks at Milo. "How do you ask for money from the man who gave you back your son?"

Milo did not know. Only Anton and Old Teo knew. At the end of a table, Teo nods slowly.

Anton takes out his own copy of the paper and tears it in two. Then he gives Beno back his field.

"This week I asked because I was afraid for my mill," Anton says. "That is my shame, not yours."

He sits down. Beno picks up the accordion. Lina and Milo start the first dance.

Late that night, you put your father's copy in the oven. Only the front. You keep the back, with his words.

"Pay this before any of you marries." In the end, you all did. Together.

screens:
Sunday. Four in the morning. The oven is hot. The red book is open at Wedding Bread.

You bake alone. Beno left last night without a word. You heard his steps go up the hill.

By noon, the square is full. Three hundred people at the long tables. Lights in the walnut tree. Your bread is on every table, still warm.

Lina walks out in white. The whole village stands up.
Beno sits at the far end of the last table, with his children. He does not look at the head table. His accordion stays in its case.

You give the toast. Your hands shake. You talk about your father, his red book, and the bread. You say nothing about the paper.

When you sit down, Anton is standing.

The square goes quiet. "Before the first dance," Anton says. Everyone waits.

He takes a paper out of his pocket. His copy. He holds it up. Then he walks over and puts it in your hand.

"You decide," he says, so only you can hear. Then, loud, to everyone: "The baker's family owes me nothing. Dance."

The music starts. People talk again. Nobody knows what just happened. You don't either.

Late at night, you find Anton on the bridge by the mill, alone.

"Why?" you ask. "Twenty-two years. Why did you never ask?"

He looks down at the water. "The summer after your father signed, my boy fell into the river by the mill wheel. He was four. I could not reach him. Your father was bringing the bread. He jumped in."

"How do you ask for money from the man who gave you back your son?"

"This week I asked because I was afraid for my mill. That is my shame, not yours."

He walks home. You stand on the bridge with both papers in your hand.

Back in the square, someone is folding the chairs in the dark, one by one. It is Beno.

You put both papers in your pocket. You start walking toward him.

screens:
Sunday. Four in the morning. The oven is hot. The red book is open at Wedding Bread.

Beno stayed all night. He shapes every loaf with you. Small bread, for a small wedding.

At ten, you walk to the mill with your mother's tin. Half. You put it on Anton's desk.

He looks at it. He does not open it. He puts it under his arm and walks back with you.
At noon, the family stands in the bakery yard. Twenty people. Lina in white. Milo in his father's old suit. Anton and his wife stand by the gate, the tin still under his arm.

Then the gate opens. The woman from the café comes in with a pot of soup. Behind her, the postman with a cake. Behind him, half the village. Then the other half.

Nobody was invited. Everybody came. Each one carries a plate.

By one o'clock, the yard is full, and the street, and the square. Three hundred people eat from their own pots. Your little loaves are torn and shared, one between ten.

Beno climbs onto a chair with his accordion.

But before he plays, he says it, to everyone. "My brother paid my debt, 22 years ago. I let him carry it. I am sorry."

Nobody claps. Nobody looks away either.

Then Old Teo gets up from his chair, slowly. He points his stick at Anton. "Tell them," he says. "Or I will."

Anton's face goes red. He does not speak. So Teo does.

"The summer after they signed, Anton's boy fell into the river by the mill wheel. Four years old. Anton could not reach him. Elias was bringing the bread. He jumped in."

"That is why Anton never asked. How do you ask for money from the man who gave you back your son?"

Milo turns to his father. Anton nods. Just once.

Then he walks to Lina and puts your mother's tin in her hands. "A wedding gift," he says. "A real one."

Beno plays. Lina and Milo dance in the bakery yard, between the soup pots.

That night, you open the red book. Under Wedding Bread, in your own hand, you write: Feeds 300, if everyone brings something.

screens:
Sunday. Four in the morning. The oven is hot. The red book is open at Wedding Bread.

You bake alone. Small bread, for a small wedding. Beno left last night without a word.

At ten, you walk to the mill with your mother's tin. Half. You put it on Anton's desk.

He opens it. He does not count. He just looks at the coins for a long time.

"Your father tried to pay me," he says. "Every year. Every year I said no."

"Why?"

He closes the tin. "Today I tell my son. Then he can tell you."

At noon, the family stands in the bakery yard. Twenty people. Lina in white. Milo in his father's old suit. Anton and his wife by the gate.

Beno is not there. His children are.

You give the toast. It is short. You say what your father always said: "Bread first. Then everything else."

Lina laughs and cries at the same time.
Before the first dance, Anton takes Milo out into the street. They are gone for ten minutes. When Milo comes back, his face is wet. He comes straight to you.

"When I was four, I fell into the river by the mill wheel," he says. "I never knew. Your father jumped in. He pulled me out."

"That is why my father never asked. He says: how do you ask for money from the man who gave you back your son?"

At the gate, Anton holds up the tin. "Half in coins," he says to you. "The other half your father paid in the river, long ago. We are even."

Then Lina and Milo dance, in a yard with twenty people. It is enough.

Late at night, you walk up the hill with one loaf of bread. Beno's light is on.

You stand at his door for a long time. You put the bread on the step. You do not knock. Not yet.

Halfway down the hill, you hear his door open behind you.

You do not turn round. But you walk a little slower.
